name: Amira Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Amira. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yes, that's fine. I like talking about this, honestly. Most people on site just roll their eyes.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a roofing carpenter for Ashby Homes, a house builder, so I put up the roof timbers on new houses. Some roofs are trusses that come ready-made from a factory, and some we cut by hand from straight timber, which is the bit I love. A typical day is up on the scaffold by eight, measuring, cutting rafters, nailing, checking the line. What wears me out is the wind and the cold up there, and the fact that the pay hasn't moved in two years.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about money and the rest of your life outside work.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live on my own in a studio above a laundrette, so it's warm at least. I've got a weekend side thing building decks and the odd garden room, and I use AI every day to work out roof pitches and write quotes. But I bought a good mitre saw on credit last year and I still owe on it, so I've only got about two weeks of money saved. There aren't many building firms near here, and Ashby is the big one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So the AI I already use stays about as good as it is. That's fine, it's useful as it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm a bit disappointed, I was hoping for more. I'd still tell people it's worth using for the boring maths. Online I'd post a picture of a deck and say the AI wrote my quote, not my roof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my problem isn't AI. I still owe eleven hundred on the saw I bought on credit, so a quiet AI future doesn't make my bank balance any less scary. Ashby's pay is stuck and there's nowhere else to go nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the decking side harder, aiming for one job every other weekend through spring and summer. I'd pay off the saw by next autumn and then start saving. I'd also ask Ashby about a pay review, since I've been there four years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Restless more than worried. A bit uneasy about money, that's all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say in the pay review?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I can cut a hip roof faster than anyone on the gang and I've trained two apprentices. I'd bring the numbers, how many roofs I did this year. They'd probably give me a little bit, not much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever go full time on the decking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One day, maybe. Not with two weeks saved and a loan. I'd need at least three months put away first.

say: She's a bit **disappointed** AI didn't do more.
AI is still worth using for the **boring maths** and writing quotes.
think: Her real problem is a **saw loan** and **stuck pay**.
There's **nowhere else** nearby to take her skills.
do: Build a **deck** every other weekend through spring and summer.
Pay off the **saw loan** by next autumn, then save.
Ask Ashby for a **pay review** after four years.
S0.quote: I still owe eleven hundred on the saw I bought on credit, so a quiet AI future doesn't make my bank balance any less scary.
fieldNote: Job looks safe, but **debt** and thin savings keep her **uneasy**.

Would argue her case with **numbers** in a pay review.

steps.text: Build a deck every other weekend through spring and summer
Pay off the mitre saw loan by next autumn
Ask Ashby Homes for a pay review after four years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, so the thinking jobs change first. My roofs are safe for a while, my side business gets easier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should learn the tools now, it's not that hard. I'd tell the lads on site that the office at Ashby will change long before the scaffold does. I'd post my roof calculator setup online so others can copy it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the AI already does my roof maths and writes my decking quotes, so for a one-woman weekend business this picture is mostly good news. The risk is Ashby cutting site managers and loading more on us. But I'd be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use AI to handle bookings and invoices for the decking, so I could do more jobs. I'd learn the 3D design software builders use, which AI makes easier to learn. I'd raise my decking prices a bit because my quotes would look more professional.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quite good, actually. Excited with a little nervousness.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at Ashby?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kev, the site manager, who spends half his day on paperwork and ordering. If the software does that, Ashby might not need three of him. He's been decent to me, so that'd be sad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be fine. With two weeks saved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair point. Fine in the job, I mean. Money's still tight, but this picture makes the side work pay better, so it helps.

Ashby's **office** will change long before the scaffold does.
think: AI already does her **roof maths** and **quotes**, so this is good news.
Ashby may cut **site managers** and load more work on carpenters.
do: Use AI for **bookings and invoices** on decking jobs.
Learn **3D design** software with AI help.
Raise **decking prices** on the back of better quotes.
S1.quote: The AI already does my roof maths and writes my decking quotes, so for a one-woman weekend business this picture is mostly good news.
fieldNote: Sees Steady Disruption as an **opportunity** for her side business.
Admits being **fine** means the job, not the money, so **uneasy**, not calm.
Feels for **Kev**, whose paperwork-heavy role is exposed.

steps.text: Use AI to handle decking bookings and invoices
Learn 3D design software with an AI tutor
Raise decking prices by a tenth with more professional quotes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2028, and robots on roofs by 2031. That's quick. I'd be 32.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say don't panic, get in early. Workers who learn to run the machines will be fine for a while. I'd also say the government should help people who can't move as fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, if a robot can cut a roof by 2031, I want to be the woman who owns the robot, not the woman it replaced. But owning one costs money I don't have. So really I'd be scrambling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year, I'd get trained on the roof-truss factory machines at Ashby's supplier, so I'm on the robot side early. I'd keep the decking going and save every penny for a deposit on equipment. I'd look at drone roof surveys too, because flying a drone is hands-on and in demand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous and fired up at the same time. Like the start of a race when you've got the wrong shoes on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said owning one costs money. How would you get there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a small business loan, or going in with someone. My friend Priya is an electrician and we've talked about doing garden rooms together. Two of us could maybe afford one machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in 2028, before the robots, when the thinking side changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Let the AI do all my quotes, plans and ordering, so I can take more decking jobs and build savings. The three years in between are my window. After 2031 it's a different game.

The **government** should help people who can't move as fast.
think: She wants to **own the robot**, not be replaced by it.
Owning one costs money she **doesn't have**.
do: Train on **truss factory machines** at Ashby's supplier this year.
Look into **drone roof surveys** as hands-on work.

fieldNote: Adaptive and eager, but **no capital**, so **anxious**, not calm.

Thinks of teaming up with Priya to **buy a machine**.

steps.text: Train on the truss factory machines at Ashby's supplier

Use AI for every quote, plan and order

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots by 2034. That gives me three more years than the last one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is plenty if you start now. I'd tell the apprentices to learn the software and a second skill. I'd post what I'm doing so other women in trades can see it's possible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be 34 when the robots come, which is young enough to start again and old enough to be tired of starting again. Five years is enough for a plan but not enough to save much on Ashby's pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd do a drone pilot licence and start offering roof surveys alongside decks. By year three I'd want the garden room business with Priya registered and earning. I'd pay off every debt before 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Determined, a bit tired thinking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the apprentices exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn to cut a roof by hand, because it teaches you how a roof works. Then learn the software, because that's where the jobs move. Don't skip either one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to Ashby in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd buy robots around 2034 and keep a few of us to check the work. I'd rather be gone by then, on my own terms. If I'm still there, I'm one of the people they choose between.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. 2039 for robots. That's a whole career stage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this one is the chance to do it properly. I'd tell people to treat it like a ten-year plan. I wouldn't go on about doom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is enough to turn my weekend decking jobs into a real firm, robots and all. By 2039 I'd want to be running two or three robots, not up a scaffold in the wind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build up the decking and garden rooms slowly over three years, then go full time once I had six months saved. I'd invest in good tools and later in one machine. I'd use AI for every bit of admin from day one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm. A little uneasy, but mostly I'd be looking forward.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could stop that plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bad winter with no work, or getting hurt on a roof. I've got no sick pay to speak of. One fall and the whole plan's gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stay at Ashby while you build it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, for at least three years. Ashby pays the rent, the decking pays the dream. I'd only leave once the numbers say so.

She wouldn't go on about **doom** with workmates or online.

By 2039 she'd want to **run robots**, not climb scaffolds.

Save **six months** of costs before leaving Ashby.

fieldNote: A decade turns her side work into a **business plan**: **uneasy**, close to calm.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have three years to get from broke to owning machines, and that's not enough. What would help is cheap loans for workers starting their own firms, and grants for training on the new kit.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about money to start things. I don't mind the machines. I mind being broke while everyone tells me to be brave about them.

headlineQuote: I don't mind the machines. I mind being broke while everyone tells me to be brave about them.
portrait: Amira is a **27-year-old roofing carpenter** at a house builder, who loves cutting roofs by hand.
She uses **AI every day** and runs a weekend **decking** business on the side.
She has about **two weeks** saved and still owes on a saw she bought on credit.
She wants to **own robots**, not be replaced, but lacks the money to start.
Her mood stays **uneasy to anxious**, rising only when time is short.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because three years isn't enough to go from **broke** to owning machines.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap loans** for workers starting firms and **training grants** for new kit.
